Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

# Summary of Political Manifesto

This manifesto presents a vision for national governance focused on several key policy areas, emphasising action over rhetoric and accountability in government.

## Economic Policy

The document advocates for fiscal responsibility, arguing that government spending has become excessive and unsustainable. It proposes £12 billion in annual savings through reducing civil service posts and cutting public bodies. Of these savings, £8 billion would reduce borrowing while £4 billion would fund tax cuts. The manifesto commits to maintaining central bank independence for interest rate decisions and opposes adopting a common European currency.

Pensioner support features prominently, including proposals to halve council tax for over-65s, increase state pensions in line with earnings rather than prices, and create new savings accounts with government contributions.

## Education

The manifesto emphasises school discipline as fundamental to effective learning. It proposes giving head teachers full control over admissions and expulsions, with disruptive pupils directed to specialist schools. Teachers would receive protection from malicious allegations and reduced paperwork.

Funding would follow pupils, allowing parental choice to drive resources. The document proposes 600,000 additional school places, vocational grants for teenagers, and scrapping university tuition fees. It advocates for rigorous examination standards and curriculum reform.

## Healthcare

Healthcare spending would increase to £2,000 per head annually. The manifesto proposes abolishing centrally-set targets, reducing administrative bodies, and giving hospitals freedom over staffing and investment. Patients and GPs would choose care providers, with funding following patient choices. Infection control receives particular attention, with proposals to reinstate ward matrons with authority to close wards for cleaning.

## Crime and Security

The document proposes recruiting 5,000 additional police officers annually, establishing elected local police commissioners, and implementing zero-tolerance neighbourhood policing. Prison capacity would expand by 20,000 places, with sentences served in full. Drug treatment programmes would expand significantly, including 25,000 residential rehabilitation places.

## Immigration

The manifesto proposes establishing a unified border control force, implementing 24-hour port surveillance, and introducing an Australian-style points system for work permits. It advocates withdrawing from certain international agreements to establish national control over asylum policy, processing applications outside the country, and setting annual immigration limits determined by parliament.

## Governance and Constitutional Matters

Proposals include abolishing regional assemblies, returning powers to local authorities, reducing parliamentary seats by 20 per cent, and ensuring that legislation affecting only one constituent nation is decided by representatives from that nation alone. The manifesto commits to reforming the upper legislative chamber through increased elected membership.

## Foreign Policy and Defence

Defence spending would increase by £2.7 billion for front-line forces. The document opposes a proposed European constitutional treaty, promising a referendum within six months, and commits to negotiating return of certain regulatory powers from European institutions. International development spending would increase toward 0.7 per cent of national income by 2013.

## Environment and Transport

Environmental proposals include phasing out harmful chemicals, incentivising low-emission vehicles, protecting green belt land, and promoting brownfield development. Transport policy includes modernising road networks, reviewing speed cameras, and extending rail franchises to encourage private investment.

The manifesto concludes by presenting specific actions for implementation within the first day and month of taking office, emphasising immediate accountability for stated commitments.

# Summary: Britain Forward, Not Back (2005)

## Core Philosophy

This manifesto presents a governing approach centered on providing opportunity and security for all citizens in a changing world. The document emphasizes balancing economic dynamism with social justice, combining rights with responsibilities, and reforming public services while maintaining universal access.

## Economic Policy

The manifesto highlights economic stability achievements including continuous growth, low inflation, low interest rates, and high employment levels. Future economic policy commits to:

- Maintaining inflation targets and fiscal rules
- Continuing public investment in education and health
- Pursuing full employment with a target of 80% employment rate
- Supporting enterprise through infrastructure investment in skills, science, and transport
- Implementing efficiency savings of over £21 billion for frontline services
- Not raising basic or top income tax rates

Regional economic development receives attention through development agencies, while manufacturing and business support programs continue. Transport investment exceeds £180 billion, focusing on road, rail, and public transit improvements.

## Education

Education reforms emphasize personalized learning with goals including:

- 85% of pupils achieving basic literacy and numeracy standards by age 11
- Every secondary school becoming a specialist school
- Building Schools for the Future program for modern facilities
- Expanding apprenticeships and vocational education
- Maintaining the 50% higher education participation target
- Increasing school funding and teacher numbers

Discipline measures include zero tolerance for disruption and expanded out-of-school provision for disruptive students.

## Crime and Security

Crime policy focuses on neighborhood policing teams for every community, with nearly 13,000 additional police officers and 24,000 Community Support Officers. Measures include:

- Powers to tackle antisocial behavior
- Drug testing and treatment programs
- Restrictions on weapons including replicas and knives
- Identity cards with biometric data
- Points-based immigration system
- Counter-terrorism powers including control orders

## Healthcare

Healthcare investment has doubled since 1997 and will triple by 2008. Key commitments include:

- Maximum 18-week wait from referral to treatment
- Free hospital care based on clinical need
- Expansion of NHS capacity through foundation trusts and independent providers
- Patient choice in treatment location
- Community hospitals and primary care expansion
- Public health measures including school meal standards and workplace smoking restrictions (with exemptions for licensed premises)

## Families and Older Citizens

Family support measures include:

- Universal childcare for ages 3-14
- Sure Start Children's Centers in every community
- Extended paid maternity leave to nine months
- Child poverty reduction through tax credits
- Increased homeownership opportunities

For pensioners, the Pension Credit ensures minimum income of £109 weekly. The document commits to building consensus on pension reform addressing long-term sustainability while tackling poverty and women's disadvantages.

## International Affairs

Foreign policy emphasizes engagement through international institutions including the EU, UN, G8, and Commonwealth. Priorities include:

- Supporting a reformed European Union
- Promoting democracy and human rights globally
- Maintaining strong armed forces
- Doubling international aid with a 2013 target for 0.7% of national income
- Climate change leadership with 60% carbon reduction by 2050
- Fair trade reforms benefiting developing countries

The manifesto supports a referendum on the EU Constitutional Treaty while maintaining the economic tests for euro membership.

## Constitutional Reform

Democratic reforms include:

- House of Lords reform to remove remaining hereditary peers
- Enhanced powers for devolved administrations
- Neighborhood empowerment with community call-for-action powers
- Stronger local government with reduced bureaucracy
- Council tax control through investment and capping powers

## Quality of Life

Cultural and sporting commitments include:

- Free museum admission continuing
- Supporting the 2012 Olympic bid
- Two hours of school sports weekly for all children
- Digital switchover between 2008-2012
- Environmental improvements including kerbside recycling for all households by 2010

## Summary

The manifesto presents a comprehensive program emphasizing public service investment with reform, economic stability supporting opportunity, and active international engagement. It balances universal provision with personalization, and rights with responsibilities, while proposing continued constitutional modernization.
